title: Is Jesus the "Son of God"? The Islamic View Explained
summary: Why Islam rejects the title "Son of God" for Jesus, and the specific reasoning behind that rejection rather than just the conclusion.

body.text: A title, not just a phrase

"Son of God" is one of the most theologically loaded phrases in Christianity, and Islam's rejection of it is often the first flashpoint in a conversation with Christian family. Understanding why Islam rejects it — not just that it does — makes for a far more productive conversation than a bare denial.
The Islamic objection: taken literally, it implies begetting

The core Islamic objection is that "Son of God," read plainly, implies God literally begetting a son — a biological or generative act — which Tawhid rules out entirely, since Allah has no partner, no need, and nothing comparable to Him. Surah Al-Ikhlas, covered in Stage 1, states this directly: God "neither begets nor is born." This is the theological center of the Islamic objection, not a rejection of Jesus' greatness or importance.

body.translation: It is not befitting for Allah to take a son; exalted is He! When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.

body.text: A fair note on how many Christians actually understand the title

Most Trinitarian Christian theology does not intend "Son of God" as a literal, biological claim either — it's understood as describing an eternal relationship within the Godhead, not physical generation in time. This is a genuine point of nuance worth knowing: the Islamic objection is strongest against a literal, generative reading of the title, and a well-informed Christian conversation partner will likely clarify they don't hold that literal reading either. Even so, Islam maintains that describing Jesus as sharing in God's own nature and being — however the relationship is technically defined — still crosses the line Tawhid draws, regardless of whether "begetting" is meant literally or metaphysically.

Islam affirms Jesus as a Prophet and Messenger, born miraculously of a virgin by God's direct command, given real miracles, and given the elevated titles covered in an earlier lesson — but as a created being, entirely distinct from the Creator, not sharing in God's own nature. "Servant of God" (Abdullah) is the term Islamic tradition uses in deliberate contrast to "Son of God" — the Quran describes Jesus using this term about himself, even as an infant.

body.question: Isn't rejecting "Son of God" the same as saying Jesus doesn't matter in Islam?
body.answer: No — the previous lesson in this collection covers just how honored Jesus is in the Quran (a Prophet, the Messiah, born of a virgin, worker of miracles). Rejecting his divinity specifically is not the same as rejecting his importance; Islam holds both positions at once, honoring him highly while denying he shares in God's nature.

body.question: How can I explain this to Christian family without sounding dismissive of what they believe?
body.answer: Leading with what Islam affirms about Jesus — his virgin birth, his miracles, his status as one of the greatest prophets — before explaining the specific point of disagreement tends to land far better than opening with the rejection itself; most Christian family members are more receptive when they can see the respect is genuine and specific, not a blanket dismissal.

body.question: Does understanding the specific reasoning behind Islam's rejection of "Son of God" — rather than just the conclusion — change how you'd explain it to someone who raised you Christian?
